title: Plastic-Free Flasks & Fair Trackers: How I Run Low-Impact Private Journeys
excerpt: Refillable flasks instead of plastic bottles, fair pay for village cooks and trackers, and engine-off wildlife sightings — the small, practical commitments behind every Serendiva journey.

cover.alt: Hands planting an endemic sapling on a misty Knuckles forest ridge

content:
Sri Lanka is small, beautiful and fragile. Tourism has brought jobs to many villages I love, but also plastic on beaches, traffic jams of jeeps around a single leopard and money that rarely reaches the people who make a place special. Running a one-guide business gives me the freedom to do things differently. These are the commitments I keep on every journey.

## Zero single-use plastic in the vehicle

A typical traveller in Sri Lanka uses two or three plastic water bottles a day. Over a two-week trip for a couple, that is close to a hundred bottles.

### What I do instead

- Every guest receives a double-walled stainless steel flask on the first day.
- The vehicle carries large refill containers of filtered water, topped up at hotels.
- Snacks come in reusable boxes, and king coconuts — nature's own packaging — are bought from roadside sellers.

## Fair pay, paid directly

The cook who welcomes you into her village kitchen, the tracker who finds your leopard, the stilt fisherman who poses at sunset: they are the heart of your journey. I pay them directly and fairly, agreed in advance, rather than through a chain of agents who take most of it.

### Choosing partners

I work with family-run guesthouses, community cooking programmes, handloom weavers in the Dumbara valley and local naturalists. I avoid "gem museums" and spice shops that pay commissions to guides — you will never be taken anywhere for my benefit.

## The ethical safari standard

On every wildlife drive we follow the same rules:

1. Engine off at sightings, voices low.
2. No off-road driving and no chasing animals.
3. We leave a sighting if it becomes crowded.
4. No elephant rides, no elephant shows, no feeding wild animals.
5. Whale watching with small, licensed boats that respect distance limits.

These rules sometimes mean waiting longer. They always mean better encounters.

## Supporting conservation

A share of each journey supports projects I know personally: reforestation of degraded ridges in the Knuckles range, marine research off the southern coast and a small turtle hatchery that releases hatchlings straight to the sea. Guests who wish can plant a sapling themselves on the way through the hill country.

## Small things that add up

- Hotels chosen for good water and energy practices where possible.
- Long stays instead of one-night stops, which means less driving.
- Respectful dress and behaviour at temples — I brief every guest on arrival.
- Photographs of people only with permission.

## Questions guests often ask

### Does low-impact mean less comfort?

Not at all. You still travel in a private air-conditioned vehicle and stay in beautiful places. The difference is in the details — who cooks your lunch, how we behave around wildlife and what we leave behind.

### Can we offset our flights?

I am happy to recommend certified local reforestation projects, but I always say honestly that the best thing we can do together is travel slowly, stay longer and spend locally.

## Travelling lightly with me

Responsible travel should never feel like a lecture. Most of my guests simply notice that the journey feels more personal, the people they meet are genuinely glad to see them and the places they visit still feel wild.

If these values matter to you too, [let's plan your journey together](/contact) — gently, privately and with care for the island.
